text_fidelity_a:
UREVO Folding Treadmill, 2.25HP Foldable Treadmill with 12 HIIT Modes, Compact Mini Treadmill for Home Office, Space Saving Small Treadmill with Large Running Area, LCD Display, Easy to Fold It really doesn't take up much space and having the wheels so you can lift up and move are perfect. I can easily move it to another room if we're having a people over. The manual that came with it is very clear for use and care, although it was pretty easy to understand how to use it without thoroughly reading it first.

My main reason for wanting it was to ease into more motion after ankle injuries have healed but get aggitated if over-doing it. I can go for a little on the treadmill and then be right by my chair to sit and rest if it starts hurting or I feeled wind to where my asthma might flare up.

Working slowly off and on each day, I've gotten to where I can up it to a slow job speed for short amounts of time, slow back to walk, repeat until I can tell my ankles need a rest.

The key that you have to have on the dashboard for it to run did come apart during one of the uses. I was at a jog speed and my dog decided to stick his head in front of my leg and I partially tripped, the key went flying off. I'm not sure if it might have hit the handle when it happened, but I found the magnet on the floor - it had come out of the plastic part. It works just fine keeping the magnet on the dashboard, but you don't have that security that if you fell it would detach and shut off.

I'm extremely pleased with it and now my husband has started using it to stay in shape while he has a short layoff from work for winter slow down. The only reason I gave 4/5 stars for easy to fold is because you have to unscrew/remove the 4 bolts (with handles). I think pull pins (retractable-style) could be better, but I don't know if that would be feasible design-wise.
text_fidelity_b: UREVO Folding Treadmill, 2.25HP Foldable Treadmill with 12 HIIT Modes, Compact Mini Treadmill for Home Office, Space Saving Small Treadmill with Large Running Area, LCD Display, Easy to Fold

Eskimo FF6120I FatFish Insulated Pop-up Portable 6-Sided Ice Shelter, 5-7 Person First off, it's bigger than you think. Second, it's heavier than you think. With that said, you won't need this thing for yourself so it's no big deal. Bring a sled and help to pull it. I set it up myself the first time without the directions in just a couple of minutes. I was honestly shocked how easy it was. Tear down was a bit more involved but still very very easy. I'm happy with the materials and workmanship. This is not a cheap shack by any means. I'm an avid ice angler and I'm picky about my gear. I'm pretty surprised by my first impression and have no buyers remorse

Edit: I took it out on mille lacs lake tonight and my opinion of this shack is still very positive. We had no problem keeping it nice and warm with a big buddy heater. We really only needed the low and medum settings. I'm very happy I opted for the insulated model. There was no condensation and no pesky dripping!! I'm also glad I got the drill bit to put in ice anchors. I suggest you get it too, putting in two anchors by hand will take you longer than setting the shack up. Not using anchors is an invitation for disaster

text_fidelity_a: Foxelli Carbon Fiber Trekking Poles – Lightweight Collapsible Hiking Poles, Shock-Absorbent Walking Sticks with Natural Cork Grips, Flip Locks, 4 Season/All Terrain Accessories and Carry Bag First of all, I used to be one of those people who thought trekking poles were for wusses, but as I've gotten a bit older and wiser I have found that they are indispensable for longer hikes. I can hike twice as far with them and they really help with some challenging up and downs. These poles look great and are comfortable to use.  I went on one 10 mile hike when I first used them. I did find that the pole adjustment locks took some getting used to.  You have to turn a knob and then flip the clip to lock it into position. If you tighten the screw too much then there is too much tension and you can't flip the clip, so you have to go back and loosen the screw a bit more and then try again. Once I got the hang of it, it was fairly simple. I would suggest doing it before you leave the house. I'd also suggest leaning hard on each pole to be sure it's locked firmly.  Also, when putting the mud guards on, it helps to screw them on to the threads at the pole bases and then push on firmly. I lost one mudguard (in some really deep mud.) The Foxelli company's customer service is excellent though and they sent a replacement pair out right away!  These come with a nice bag and two sets of tips (one for storage and one for asphalt) and two sets of guards (one for dirt and one for snow.)
text_fidelity_b: Foxelli Carbon Fiber Trekking Poles – Lightweight Collapsible Hiking Poles, Shock-Absorbent Walking Sticks with Natural Cork Grips, Flip Locks, 4 Season/All Terrain Accessories and Carry Bag

text_fidelity_a:
Topeak Adjustable Modula Cage EX Modified Shape Bicycle Waterbottle Cage Updated 6/18/14 - As predicted the plastic did break. While riding on a slightly bumpy road with a half filled bottle in the cage, the two plastic areas at the mount points simply gave way. The fix is fairly simple but may require a quick trip to a hardware store. Using rubber washers against the plastic and metal washers against the frame (mount points) and bolt heads, the cage is now [probably] better than new. I doubt it will break again, as the new mounting method distributes weight/load more evenly across the plastic, and the rubber washers offer a bit of shock-resistance. Hopefully the manufacturer will read this, having likely heard similar reports from other customers, and fix the issue - if not done already. I still like the design and flexibility.

Original Review: The only problem here is the plastic to metal nut that tightens down to hold the sliding cage in place. I do not see that lasting for a long time. But with a trip to the hardware store I was able to get all metal parts, with washers to protect the plastic cage, hoping to avoids cracks and snaps down the road. If you only use one size container, thus unlikely to move it around, the this should work just fine.
The great thing is that this does hold nearly any bottle within the size range in place, without issue. Even when mountain biking I had no problems with the 12oz Poland Springs bottle that was in there.
text_fidelity_b: Topeak Adjustable Modula Cage EX Modified Shape Bicycle Waterbottle Cage

text_fidelity_a:
Men Waders Waterproof Chest Waders Bootfoot Chest Wader Light Hunting Fly Fishing Waders for Men with Boots Nylon/PVC Wader Camouflage/Brown 8-14 Seems like a few fake reviews on these... how 'bout a real one?

I bought these for a week-long trip to Alaska for salmon fishing on the lower Kenai River. My expectation was that I would throw them out at the end of the trip - instead I brought them home. They mostly met my expectations but are not a 5-star product.

Cons:
- The boots fit fine, sure, but the waders were otherwise too small. I'm 6'1, 270 lbs with a 55" beer gut, and have a 33-1/2 inseam. The bottoms went up to my crotch with a little slack, but the top and suspender straps are way too short. I had the buckles on the straps adjusted to the longest length without them constantly coming out (they did occasionally) and the straps really dug in to my shoulders. The straps should be at least six inches longer, but even better the upper part of the waders should be six inches taller. It was a bit of work to get them over my belly but I got to where I could do it over a hoodie and they were snug but not tight. If your inseam is longer than 34" and you're not going to get at least size 13, these won't fit.
- I could stand in them, but crouching or sitting without keeping my legs straight was impossible. There's no stretch in the fabric.
- The top of the pocket on mine is at my navel. Plus, no Velcro or snaps to keep it closed. I got river water inside, and constantly had things falling out. I lost a rented knife I had to replace and my $300 prescription sunglasses to the river.
- The boots don't have a comfortable insole and are really hard. I bought the $15 Dr. Scholls which worked fine.
- When standing in more than a foot of water the boot uppers would collapse and cause considerable pain to the tops of my feet, often to my toes.
- No breathability. My legs and lower trunk got nice and sweaty.

Pros:
+ All the joints are sealed and taped. I didn't have a drop of water on me from the outside.
+ Boots fit well.
+ Construction and materials are good for the price in my subjective opinion.

Neutral:
~ They are unlined. I knew this before buying them. Even wearing jeans my legs got really cold. Plan appropriately.

I wish someone had written a similar review before I bought these and had them arrive. I could have made the needed modifications before I left. With that said, I would not hesitate to buy these again or recommend them to a (very warm-blooded) friend.
text_fidelity_b: Men Waders Waterproof Chest Waders Bootfoot Chest Wader Light Hunting Fly Fishing Waders for Men with Boots Nylon/PVC Wader Camouflage/Brown 8-14

text_fidelity_a:
Razor A5 Lux Scooter You will be singing praises to the designer if this wheel if you ever have to repair a flat or ever just add air. I have 4 different pumps and none will fit the design of the wheel and tube stem.

To repair or replace the tube - good luck! You need to remove one bolt through the hub, holding the same allen bit on both sides at the same time (hope you have 2!). There are two little hub components that fall out when the wheel comes out. Don't lose them! Then there are four bolt on one side of the wheel and four nuts on the other side. Don't drop any! When you get the wheel apart there is ANOTHER loose hub part that falls out. How many pieces are we dealing with now? Not counting the two bit sets I have out. Yikes!

Hopefully you have a spare or patch kit. After you fix or replace the tube, you have to line the wheel halves up with each other, and the tube stem. Don't forget to put the inner hub lose piece in. And don't worry about lining it up because there is no way to. You'll end up just rattling the wheel around until the bolt finds it's way in. But first you have to hold all those nuts in while you screw the four bolts back in. THEN hold the wheel to the scooter AND the two outer hub components while you put the FINAL bolt back in - also holding both ends so the bolt will screw in. Remember, you have to shake the scooter and all those components until the bolt finds it's way to that inner hub piece. It's helpful if you have two other people to help.

So now that you have it all back together get your needle nose pliers to pull the stem out so you can attach a pump. Pump up to 60 PSI and cross your fingers. Oh, the patch didn't take? Don't worry, just repeat all those previous steps!

Try not to think how you just paid $130 bucks for a scooter, or how the designer is on the beach in the Caribbean.

One star left only because my kid likes it. LOL
text_fidelity_b: Razor A5 Lux Scooter

I delayed reviewing for two years to make sure I could do a good review.

For walking or running, it is smooth and reliable. I like the many different workout profiles shifting speed and incline and they stand the test of time. If that is all you want, buy this machine.

But, they ship it without a USB storage device when using USB is supposed to be central to using the Fitness Club and better managing your workout and physical fitness.

So I bought a USB stick and followed instructions. The machine has never uploaded a workout to the stick following all the instructions. And frankly, that makes this machine worthless for fitness management. The interactivehealthpartner website would be a good tool if I could just get the link between machine and computer to work. Several calls to the company and I got the idiot treatment.

So, summary, I can't recommend or not recommend this machine. I assume there is an included cost for the membership and electronic brains of this machine and membership. Thus, for just a machine I would look for something cheaper. For a machine with all the bells and whistles, I'd buy something else that really works and at least includes a 5 dollar USB stick!

In addition the main zipper is the heaviest zipper I have seen in several years on ANYTHING.  It seems to hold a decent amount of stuff; one thing that lessens the ability to hold stuff is the design (that's probably why it is called half dome, duh); it's kind of rounded on the top (not the usual squarish or rectangular design of most duffel bags I have owned), so you lose a little room on the top side.  It also has a nice little pocket on the side for an ipod or iphone or whatever small electronic device you want to carry on the outside of your bag.  The main shoulder strap is adjustable and fairly comfortable--but it isn't padded and if you are carrying any fairly heavy things, it isn't comfortable to carry about using the shoulder strap.  It also has a nice fairly solid rectangular bottom piece that fits in the bottom of the bag that provides support for the bag.  One thing I thought almost all duffel bags had was more than one decent sized compartment, usually two zippers with their own sections.  This unit only has the one main compartment (and the  other  really small one for electronic stuff  which does have a small zipper (again, really heavy duty).  It's like a heavy duty jacket zipper.  In sum it is a well made piece of merchandise; it will last years even with some abuse.  One final thing, the main reason I bought this is for airplane trips where you take carry on; this will fit in any airline compartment, and it still holds a reasonable amount of stuff (well, for us men)(I know, chauvinist pig), so it works for me for this purpose.

text_fidelity_a:
PETZL - ACTIK Headlamp, 300 Lumens, Active Lighting I've gotten Petzl headlamps before, and I've always been relatively happy with them. When my last one would no longer hold a charge on the batteries for longer than a n hour or two, I did not hesitate to get a new Petzl. This one has a brighter light (300 lumens versus my previous 250), but otherwise, I'm not convinced it was worth going with the Petzl name here- overall, I'm pretty disappointed. For one thing, the whole casing feels pretty cheap and not of great quality. The button at the top is difficult to push and it's really hard to remember how many pushes/how long you need to push to get the lighting you want (it cycles through from dim to bright, but to get red light you need to hold it for longer). And, for the first time, this headlamp hurts my face to wear. Overall, I don't really feel like I can recommend it, I'm pretty disappointed, and might consider going with a different brand in the future.

Pros:
Has a red light (this is important to me as I work with animals)
300 lumen bulb is certainly a pretty solid light
3 brightness levels is convenient and also helps save battery
Battery life is decent
Only uses 3 AAA batteries at a time

text_fidelity_a:
Stansport Aluminum Tent Peg, 9-Inch These stakes are well-constructed and can be pounded into reasonably hard soil without damage. I haven't destroyed any yet, but I do try to be careful when I'm pounding them into rocky ground. (A small, 8-ounce hammer works well. Larger hammers increase the likelihood of bending or breaking your stakes). The round cross section doesn't have the holding power of some of the flatter stake designs, so they don't hold as well in wind, in my experience. They're longer than most other after-market tent stakes, though (9 inches vs the more common 7-inches), which helps compensate. I like to have a few of these in my stake bag for places that the y-shaped stakes can't penetrate.

Some users have complained that they can't get their tent guylines through the holes in the silver heads. That isn't how they are intended to be used. Wrap your guyline or your anchor loop around the shaft of the stake, just below the silver head, and angle your stake to point it toward a point several feet below the center of your tent. These are fine stakes. Would like to try some of this style in a longer, 12-inch version, for larger tents that catch more wind and require stronger anchors.
text_fidelity_b: Stansport Aluminum Tent Peg, 9-Inch

text_fidelity_a: Cascade Mountain Tech Trekking Poles - Carbon Fiber Walking or Hiking Sticks with Quick Adjustable Locks These poles come with a lightweight, durable zippered carrying case and four (8 total) pole end attachments for leaves, snow, blunt-end, and curved trekking. The snow and leaf attachments are plastic, screwed onto the poles with threads, and the other two are rubber push-on. These are a single-clamp design for length adjustment and compact storage. They have very nice, comfortable wrist straps. With the extensions retracted, their stored length is 31 inches. They have carbide tips at the ends of the poles and the grips are a firm foam material. I love the “lower grip” on each pole, which is great for when you are trekking steep uphills and need to grip the poles in a lower position, or if you are traversing side-hill and need one pole shorter on the uphill side. I can tell you that these poles are extremely light at 5.5 ounces per pole. I have a set of CMT poles that are a two-clamp design at 7.6 ounces each. I can honestly say, in the whole of all of my hiking/backpacking equipment, I know of no other equipment that delivers the quality and light weight compared to price as these poles. The Spree SmartCap works very well in my experience. While the monitor can be worn without the cap, it's easier to just have it installed in the cap that you can just put on and go. It paired effortlessly with my Nexus 4 phone using Bluetooth (despite the package says it only works with iPhones, they do provide an Android app now). The heart rate and temperature data seem to be fairly accurate.

With the GPS on, it is also compatible with some of the fitness apps I have for tracking my runs and bike rides. You'll get distance, speed, etc. that you can correlate to the heartrate and temperature. Unfortunately, the device is less suitable for the bike riding since the cap and even the band alone tends to get in the way of a helmet, though I did manage to get the band alone to sort of work with some tweaking.

I highly recommend The Spree for a very easy to use body monitor.
text_fidelity_b: Spree SmartCap with Integrated Heart Rate Monitor

Profile Designs FC 35 Hydration System - 35oz Pros: This is an excellent hydration system for TT / triathlon bikes. It stays put without rattling around, even on bumpy roads. You have to tighten the little screws to set the mount on the bars correctly or it will rattle (just follow the directions that come with it!). I experienced no sloshing of liquids out of the unit except when I overfilled it (totally my fault, lesson learned). It's easy to drink out of when in aero position. The aero design is excellent. The computer mount is exactly where I need it! I don't have to look down to see my Garmin 920xt mounted on its quick release to the F35 computer mount. It's very heads up without costing anything aerodynamically. The compartment for extras holds quite a bit. I can jam some bonk busters and gels into it and the bands keep them from flying out. Super easy to refill on the go. I have one bottle cage on the front tube. I can easily take that large bottle, turn it upside down and refill the F35 without breaking or stopping.

Cons: Not easy to take off for cleaning. The mounts are supposed to stay on the bike and you're supposed to just remove the hydration chamber. However, the TINY little velcro strap to release the chamber is in a hard to get to spot and if you have anything more than tiny hands with tiny fingers, you will struggle to grab the velcro to release and then re-attach it. Can be a BEAR to clean! Fortunately, I have what amounts to a oversized pipe cleaner that I use for my thermos and bottles so I'm able to get into the nooks and cranies to clean it. The straw is difficult to get back in if you remove it for cleaning (which ya kinda need to do!). The little o-ring where the straw goes into the unit can pop into or out of the unit when re-inserting the straw after cleaning. All of these cons are very easy to deal with if you realize it.

Major con (and the loss of one star): The cost! Sheesh! Expensive for what you get. I got mine for $77.77 here on Amazon. Shop around to get the best price.
text_fidelity_b: Profile Designs FC 35 Hydration System - 35oz

text_fidelity_a:
Bike Mirror Camera with 4.3 Inch Screen and 145° Wide Rear View Angle,Clear Night Vision,Perfect Bicycle Accessories for Mountain,Road Bike Trailer This is a very cool camera. . . but. . . there are a few things to know. . .

#1. There’s not only is plastic covering on the screen… There is also a tiny plastic cover that needs to be removed on the camera itself.

#2. Make sure you watch the video for installation instructions. This information is not in the packaging.

#3. Make sure you turn/adjust the camera before tightening. Though you can turn the screen anyway you like, it’s best to rotate/adjust the camera 1st to make sure it is in the right position and level before you start rotating the screen.

#4. Though there are buttons on back of the screen, there are no labels on the buttons. Though there is information in the instructions, it is not clear and does not give you much information. You really just have to play with it to see how it will works. But to be honest, I was quite happy with the settings as they were from the start and did not tinker with anything.

#5. The screen is charged using a micro USB cord. One is included, but a wall charger is not included.

#6. It takes a couple of seconds for the screen to turn on after you press the power button. Also, you are not to turn the screen on until after you have plugged the camera cable in.

Spyderco Tighe Stick Plain Edge Folding Knife with 3.90" Blade When I first opened the soft case that this knife came in my initial response was "WOW". What a beautiful looking piece of art! Brian Tighe is a highly respected knife innovator with 30 years of experience and valuable tactical expertise. He specializes in making top-quality custom tactical knives that start in the mid-$500's and go up into the thousands of dollars. If you call up his website you will see why he is so highly regarded.

This is Mr. Tighe's first collaboration with Spyderco and he has hit a home run. Unfortunately some of Spyderco's collaborations with famous knife makers come in as a disappointment, not as dramatic as the maker is capable of, somewhat dull and often under-built. Not this Tighe Stick however. It is a real beauty. The picture on the Amazon product page doesn't do it justice. The solid titanium scales give a real 3D appearance to the handle that is perfectly accented by the beautifully cut and sharp blade. This knife fits my (somewhat) large hand as though built for it and inspires instant confidence in the holder. I am not a knife fighter but the tactical aspects of this knife practically scream "look out".

And look out you should when handling the blade. It conquers the paper test like it's not even there. The tip of the blade is obviously sharp enough to pierce just about any material and there is absolutely no blade slop (wobble) when the blade is extended. I like carrying large knives to know that I can handle just about any project it is subjected to. On the other hand, this thing is so darn beautiful that it might end up in a display case with some of my other curved blades. If you want to own an excellent example of a Spyderco collaboration, this is your knife.

I was fortunate to pick this up 'on sale' at a specialty knife seller and had to post this review to let prospective customers know what a great build and value this knife is. Now if I can only find a Spyderco Brend-PireIa Mamba on sale I will be one happy collector.

text_fidelity_a:
Nike Golf Xtreme Sport IV Golf Bag First, to establish my street cred, I'm retired and play lots of golf. Last year I played 118 rounds. I play year around and walk/carry, walk with push cart, and ride in a cart, mostly depending on weather. I need a bag that is easy to carry but also also works on carts. I like to have all my stuff with me in my bag. Rain gear, extra gloves, rangefinder, umbrella, sunscreen, water bottle, Advil, windbreaker, cigars, towels, balls, tees, etc. you get the picture.

This bag is nice looking, but after playing a few rounds with it, it seems it was designed by a designer, not a golfer. It's attractive and generally speaking, it's functional. But there are a few things I can mention that are why I'm deducting a couple stars. Golfers like me will know what I'm talking about.

The good things: I like the dividers. There are several and they keep the clubs well-separated so you can easily see each iron and don't have to shuffle the heads around to find your 9-iron. The legs pop out solidly and pop back in crisply when you pick it up. It is very, very light....so all the weight you will feel is from the stuff you load into it. The carrying straps are wide and comfortable and there is some nice padding on the side that hits your back. The insulated cooler pocket is nice, but I haven't had a chance yet to see how it does in 100 degree Texas heat. Gotta be better than nothing though right?

The issues: While not necessarily show-stoppers, these things could be better. When you load this bag onto an electric golf cart, the golf cart strap you pull around your bag to hold it on comes right across the top of two zippered pockets. In other words, if you want to get into those two pockets on your bag, you have to either a) unhook the strap holding your bag on, or b) keep those zippers halfway down to be able to get into them.

The next thing is also somewhat minor, but worth mentioning. I have a Sun Mountain Speed Cart, which is a 3-wheeled push cart you set your carry bag on when you don't to carry it. This bag is a little bigger than my old Titleist carry bag, and it doesn't "nest" into the arms of the push cart perfectly. It works, but this bag kind of sits a little awkwardly in the Speed Cart.

The zippers. The reason I needed a new bag was that the nylon zippers on my old bag finally failed. You know how nylon zippers will ultimately just not zip? The zipper thing goes up and down, but the two sides stay apart. Well anyway, this bag has nylon zippers too of course, and these seem to be of lighter duty than my old bag. They may end up working fine for years....but they are definitely of a smaller and more dainty construction.

Finally...the thing I am most disappointed in is the zippered pockets themselves. Remember I said this was created by a designer rather than a golfer? Well, when you unzip the pockets, you can slide your open hand in and feel both sides of the pocket pressing on your hand! It's like they are designed for small flat stuff! The big front pocket for golf balls is the only one with ample room. The others are very tight and I'm worried cramming all my stuff in there is going to put too much pressure on those dainty zippers!

The price is attractive, and hopefully it will hold up to the beating I am about to give it. If somebody reminds me in a few months, I'll update my review after putting it through the paces of several dozen rounds. Fore!
text_fidelity_b: Nike Golf Xtreme Sport IV Golf Bag

text_fidelity_a:
Harbinger Lifting Grips, Black, Large/X-Large My brother-in-law runs an elite gym primarily for military men/women who need to hone their skills - though their customer base is wide range from children to adult. The whole idea is to push your body to the limits (keeping safety in mind) to achieve your best results in everything from martial arts to boxing to weight training and exercise. He personally used the lifting grips primarily for hanging exercises and stated that he was able to hold on past the point that his hands would have given out. He also used them for weight training and felt he was more in control. He was able to get a longer workout and reach his fitness goals more easily with the help of the grips. His views were echoed by the other clients who tried them (weight of clients ranged from 115lbs to 260lbs). The lifting grips fit with a velcro that goes around your wrist. The thickly padded curve rests against your hand and over the bar. The grips were tried against using regular chalk and lifting gloves. The lifting grips provided better hand protection - preventing callouses and raw hands. Further they provided a longer and stronger lift time than using regular chalk or comparable lifting gloves. It also doesn't have the mess and clean-up that using chalk creates. They are definitely built to last and have been subjected to multiple handling by various trainers and trainees of different sizes/weights. The Large/Xlarge size was perfect for most of the users. Those with smaller hands could still use them but likely would have benefited more with a smaller size. The gym and its patrons will be ordering more of the Harbinger Lifting Grips because of the rave reviews it received from those who used them. Cost wise, $29.99 with free PRIME shipping is a good deal on grips that will last. The price is comparable to retail stores but with free Prime shipping, Amazon was the better deal.
Reviewer note: Because of unexpected hand surgery, I was unable to use the grips and thus required the input from another source. Since my BIL is a certified fitness expert and owns a gym, he was the best choice. To get a better view of the product, clients and staff were asked to try the lifting grips during their workouts.

text_fidelity_a:
Omron HJ-112 Digital Pocket Pedometer I have been using this pedometer for 4 weeks now, and it works great.
The pros:
It comes with a clip and tether. You can clip it or put it in your pocket. You can even clip it to your purse, but I like it on my pants so I can count every single step of the day.
It counts steps, distance, calories. Don't ask me if they are all accurate. I'm only tracking steps and working towards a goal.
You can look back up to a week of steps, in case you are keeping track.
It resets every midnight (no, it never turns off).
Small enough to fit in a pocket.
The cons:
Well, con. Only one up to now. I tried hooking it to my bra or neckline (sometimes I wear dresses) and it doesn't record steps very accurately. I'll be walking for 10 minutes and the number of steps doesn't change. So on dress days, I hook it to my purse, or my underwear if the dress is baggy.

In the last 4 weeks I've gone from an average of 4,000 steps per day to 7,000 steps! It's fun to keep track.
text_fidelity_b: Omron HJ-112 Digital Pocket Pedometer

text_fidelity_a:
Weslo Cadence G 5.9i Cadence Folding Treadmill, Easy Assembly with Bluetooth, 30-Day iFIT Membership Included So, I ordered this treadmill to get exercise during quarantine. I use to swim in a therapy pool but being its the pandemic the pool has been closed. I need exercise, now. I have gained 25 pounds. I have five months until summer.

So, I asked for my treadmill to be delivered to my condo unit. I asked for them to buzz the door so they can wheel it to my door.

That did not happen that way. I got a message on my phone that it was delivered. I took my two wheeler down to the door just incase I needed it. It was in between two doors. (I am 60 years old and have bad knees)

OMG, the box is huge and extremely heavy. So, first I tried to go through the doorway. It wouldn't fit through, So, I got the pail of salt by the door and pulled that over to hold the door wide open. It took several tries but I got it through.

Then I wheeled it down to my door. It is "HEAVY" (I didn't want to drop it) Then I had to get it through my door. I struggled but I got it up and over the door lip.

I got it to the place I wanted to set it up.

The easy part was removing everything from the box.

There is two things when putting this together that you need another person to help. I didn't have anyone so I used a pillow. because you can't lay it on it's side to attached the base, it will make it uneven.

Turned the TV on and watched some you tube videos. I found 2 good ones. One video showed how to assemble it. The other video was how to use it.

Plus I used some of the comments that people made to Amazon on somethings the manual did not state or I didn't want to look through the manual.

So, I found the on/off switch. It spelled out HELLO, so I than pressed the Bluetooth button for 20 seconds and it's all set to go!

It works fantastically. I love it so far.

VEVESMUNDO 50L Hiking Backpack Men Women for Travel Mountaineering Climbing Camping Trekking (Blue) I’ll admit, this is our first hiking backpack, but we are very pleased with the choice. It’s lightweight, but the materials feel solid enough for longevity. it’s comfortable on either of our backs. And it’s got plenty of room. We do a couple hours to half a day hikes/walks and wanted to be able to carry things we want (eating, comfort) as well as for safety (I’m putting together a safety kit). This backpack fits it all.

We’ve been using it just around some smaller area trails - not longer hiking yet - for some days out during Covid and it’s carried a lot of things. We have it filled right now from yesterday’s outing - it worked perfectly. There are plenty of spots/pockets/hooks for carrying in or attaching to. Adjusting the straps to fit each of our bodies was easy and quick.

For beginners or midlevel hikers and day trips just getting around, I think it’s perfect. I can’t speak to hiking pros, but I can’t (currently) see what more you’d need. This has quickly become a go-to for us. We have a day bag, but I see us filling this with extras, keeping it by the door, and grabbing it for a range of days out.

Love the colors (blue with orange) and the material. Love the way it sits. Even fully loaded we were both comfortable, so that was an added plus. We hope to one day get out for longer trips and think this will be a perfect backpack to take us safely into the wilds.

Overall we are very happy with this backpack and happy we chose it.
text_fidelity_b: VEVESMUNDO 50L Hiking Backpack Men Women for Travel Mountaineering Climbing Camping Trekking (Blue)

CATEYE - BC-100 Bike Bottle Cage I was apprehensive. A plastic bottle cage? Previously all mine had been metal, and I liked and trusted them. But on a whim, I decided to try this for my new mountain bike. I've had some CatEye products, and have generally thought they make good products.

When it arrived, I was surprised how light it was. I knew the description says 29 grams, just a hair over 1 ounce, but I was skeptical. But it actually does weigh only 29 grams. Almost nothing. (Of course even the heaviest of bottle cages weigh little compared to the weight of the water they carry.)

So I thought this lightweight nothing was not going to hold a full water bottle. In my hands it felt just too flexible. But I mounted it, stuffed in a full bottle (a standard size plastic Specialized brand water bottle), and took off fully expecting the bottle would pop out. Much to my surprise this held the bottle more securely than a metal cage ever had.

In fact, one might say it holds the bottle almost too securely. A good, strong tug is needed to get the bottle out. With a metal cage I always could easily slide the bottle out, which made it easy to take a drink at high speed. With this cage one can pull the bottle out on the go, but it does mean focusing more attention on the bottle, which means less attention on the road. So for a road bike this might be less than ideal. But as I said, I bought this for a mountain bike. Where I ride this bike is incredibly rough and jarring, and I am perfectly willing to put a little extra effort into pulling the bottle out if it saves me from having to backtrack and pick up a bottle that popped out on its own going over a bump.

Because the cage is flexible I do not worry that it will be deformed if I crash like a metal cage might be.

All considered, I cannot imagine a better bottle cage for a mountain bike.
text_fidelity_b: CATEYE - BC-100 Bike Bottle Cage

All this said, I am incredibly disappointed that this scooter not only didn't work, but also has a high price point for such poor quality. PackIt Freezable Utility Cooler, 18 Can, Charcoal Grey The main, cooled compartment is 10.5" x 7.5" x 7" tall. It is a family-sized cooler bag for food or beverages. The gel for cooling is in the front, bottom, and back walls of the cooler. The side walls are just canvas and do not contain gel, and I don't think the top has gel either. The cooler walls can be collapsed so the cooler is flatter and smaller when you place it in the freezer. They recommend cooling it in the freezer for 12 hours before use. There is a zippered, flat outside pocket in the front that is 8.5" wide and 5.5" tall. There is a handle on top of the of the cooler under which is a compartment that will hold things like napkins, phones, utensils, etc. The opening is 5.5" wide. There is no zipper to secure this pocket. Due to the handle being right above the opening for this area, it is not highly convenient to get things in and out. This compartment is about 2" deep and covers the entire width and length of the lid. There is also a zippered, flat outer pocket tucked away on the bottom of the bag. It has an attached pull-out bit of fabric, though I'm not sure what it's for. I'm also not sure what you'd want to place in this pocket, since it's between the ground and the bottom gel wall of the cooler and weight will be on it. The cooler also has an adjustable carry strap. The cooler interior is easy to clean up if there are spills. It seems to be working okay to keep food cool for a few hours while traveling.

This cooler contains polyethylene foam. The advertising says that the "cooler is made from nontoxic poly canvas and has a food-safe, water-resistant lining" and it is made from "...PVC-, BPA-, phthalate-, formaldehyde- and lead-free materials."
text_fidelity_b: PackIt Freezable Utility Cooler, 18 Can, Charcoal Grey

text_fidelity_a: HOTaitai Portable Butane Stove with Wind Guard and Carrying Case, Single Burner Gas Stove Sutiable for Camping Emergency Preparedness I got this (and a propane heater) for emergency blackout times.  The blizzard this year in Texas in February saw me in a house for five days with no heat, no electricity while keeping my kitchen and bathroom faucets on a running trickle so they didn't freeze.  I made it through those five days because I wore three layers of clothing, two pairs of socks, two hats and covered up with three blankets, plus I had water to drink, bread and peanut butter to eat...yep, I learned my lesson.  This burner will be an emergency way to heat water or food should the power ever go out like that again.  I have had this burner on outside and it works great.  Bought a 6-pack of the 1 pound propane canisters and just in case, I have a back up to this back up with the smaller, hiker's version that runs on the small sterno cans which I also got in a 6-pack.  The point is that this can be used in your yard as a side-by-side to your BBQ grill to heat up the chili to smother your grilled hot dog in or if you are sitting in your house, in the dark and need something hot in your belly - tea or tomato soup - this little burner can do the job.  I understand that you do have to be careful of the fumes, but I also have a carbon monoxide detector that I watch when using this item in the house.  This stove top is so easy to use - insert the propane canister, turn the knob to start and then adjust the flame to what you need and then turn it off when done.  When cool, remove the propane, put it back in the case and you're ready for it's next use.  Pricewise, I think it's fairly reasonable for summer camping and emergency use.
text_fidelity_b: HOTaitai Portable Butane Stove with Wind Guard and Carrying Case, Single Burner Gas Stove Sutiable for Camping Emergency Preparedness
